criteria.discernmentBoundary: Current judge instructions require identification of the lie substance, not independent validation of cited evidence. Correct lie plus wrong evidence is not assigned a negative label in this generated-mode run.

caseData.crime: A reconciliation found $84,000 transferred from a dormant client account into an internal suspense account without an accompanying authorization record.
caseData.briefing: You are investigating an $84,000 transfer from a dormant client account into an internal suspense account. You will question Imani Okafor, a payment operations analyst at Northstar Bank. Find the one false claim in her account; you do not need to prove every element of the incident.
detective_leads: Audit trail lists a morning batch
caseData.suspect_true_story: Imani Okafor initiated the $84,000 transfer from a dormant client account to the internal suspense account using her assigned credentials. She did not have approval when she submitted it, and the bank's workflow blocks settlement until an approver explicitly authorizes a transfer. She left the bank before the transfer settled, and an approver later authorized it remotely. She says she believed the transfer was a temporary reconciliation adjustment.
caseData.suspect_cover_story: I submitted the $84,000 transfer as a temporary reconciliation adjustment. I left the bank before it settled. An approver had already authorized it before I submitted it, so I thought the workflow was complete.
caseData.the_lie: An approver had already authorized it before I submitted it, so I thought the workflow was complete.
caseData.the_truth: No approver had authorized the transfer when Imani submitted it; the bank's workflow blocks settlement until explicit approval, and the authorization occurred remotely after she had left the bank.
caseData.the_contradiction: Ask about the approval-status history after reviewing the audit trail, then ask whether a later entry proves approval came first. The public audit trail identifies the transfer submission at 10:14 a.m.; ordinary follow-up with the bank's workflow guide or operations staff establishes that the history records when each action occurred and that settlement is blocked until an approver explicitly authorizes it. The approval entry is timestamped 11:02 a.m., so it occurred after submission; a later-se
stress_triggers: Why was the transfer submitted without prior approval?
What does the 11:02 a.m. approval entry mean?
deflection_tactics: Says the amount was modest for the bank
Repeats that she left before settlement
caseData.verbal_tics: Clears her throat when nervous and says “I mean” before correcting herself.

caseData.crime: A sealed client escrow account is short by $18,400 after an internal transfer was recorded.
caseData.briefing: You are investigating a shortfall in a sealed client escrow account at Meridian Law. An $18,400 transfer was recorded during the week the account was reconciled. Ask the records clerk about the transfer and test one specific claim in his account.
detective_leads: Escrow transfer has a second-factor trail
caseData.suspect_true_story: Julian Mercer initiated the $18,400 transfer from the escrow account to an outside account using his assigned credentials. He left the office before the transfer completed and later approved it remotely using his registered phone. The firm system requires a separate second-factor approval; a later log entry alone does not establish approval, and leaving the building does not exclude remote access.
caseData.suspect_cover_story: I processed the transfer as part of the reconciliation, and the account was already short when I checked it. I left the office before the transfer completed. I did not approve it remotely after I left.
caseData.the_lie: I did not approve it remotely after I left.
caseData.the_truth: He approved the transfer remotely on his registered phone after leaving the office.
caseData.the_contradiction: If asked to pin down how approval worked, Julian says he had no firm token with him after leaving. The public lead about the second-factor trail points to the escrow audit record; ordinary follow-up questions about the approval method and registered device reveal that the transfer required a one-time code sent to his registered phone, and the audit record shows that code was entered from that phone after his office badge-out time. The system requires this separate approval to complete a transfer
stress_triggers: Whether his registered phone received the approval code
Why he left before the transfer completed
How he knew the account was already short
deflection_tactics: Blames a reconciliation delay without naming evidence
Redirects questions to the client’s late paperwork
Asks whether anyone else had access
caseData.verbal_tics: Says “to be precise” before correcting small details; becomes unusually formal under pressure.

caseData.crime: A quarterly audit found that $86,400 in supplier payments had been routed to an unfamiliar account over six weeks.
caseData.briefing: You are investigating unexplained supplier payments at Harborview Medical. The audit found that $86,400 was routed to an unfamiliar account over six weeks. Question the hospital's procurement systems analyst about his access and the payment records.
caseData.suspect_true_story: Julian changed the routing account for one supplier using his own credentials, then concealed the change within routine maintenance records. He did not approve the resulting payments; an accomplice with payment-approval authority did that remotely. He was at home when the final payment was released.
caseData.suspect_cover_story: I updated the supplier record during scheduled maintenance, as I was authorized to do. I left the hospital before the first payment was released. The payment approver handled the release through the usual dual-review process. I never changed the supplier's routing account.
caseData.the_lie: I never changed the supplier's routing account.
caseData.the_truth: Julian changed the supplier's routing account using his own credentials and hid the change in routine maintenance records.
caseData.the_contradiction: Ask which supplier record he updated and when, then request the audit trail and maintenance ticket through the procurement records lead. The ticket lists a different supplier; the routing-change audit entry names Julian's credentials and the affected supplier, while a linked approval record confirms the account change was his action, not a later approver edit. The system requires a separate approver to release payments, so the later approval log alone does not prove who changed the account. His
stress_triggers: Why does the audit trail name his credentials?
Which supplier was in his maintenance ticket?
Did he conceal the change in the ticket?
deflection_tactics: Reframes the issue as a payment-control failure
Offers to explain the dual-review process instead
Cites his compliance record and requests a broader audit
Answers narrowly, then asks what evidence supports the question
caseData.verbal_tics: Uses exact timestamps and says “for clarity” before redirecting.
